tagline: Turns a phone photo of a product into a marketplace-ready image, in batches.
verdictSummary: The pieces are all open source and all good: rembg cuts the product out, a compositor drops it onto a background, and a resize pass produces every size Amazon, Etsy and Shopify ask for. Assembling that into a batch pipeline with a preview is genuinely a sitting. What you lose is the phone. Pixelcut is used standing over a table with the product in one hand, and a desktop batch tool is a different job even when the output is identical.
coreLoopDIY: Drop a folder of product photos in, cut each one out with a local segmentation model, composite it onto a chosen background at a consistent scale and margin, and export every marketplace size in one pass.
whatYouLose: the phone app, which is where product photos are actually taken
generated backgrounds — this composites onto colours and images you supply
one-tap results on a photo you just took, with no folder involved
whyPeopleStillPay: Because ten dollars a month against standing at a desk building a pipeline is not a close call for someone whose job is selling things, not processing images.
notes: Scoped to cutout, composite and resize with no generative step, which keeps it clearly distinct from the AI-generation entries sharing this category.
prompt:
Build a batch product-photo pipeline: cutout, composite, resize. No image generation.

Input: a folder of photos, or drag and drop. Process the whole set in one run with a visible queue.

Cutout: run a local segmentation model (rembg with the u2net or isnet weights, downloaded on first use) to produce an alpha matte. Then refine it: erode the matte by a pixel to kill the halo that segmentation models leave on light backgrounds, and feather the edge slightly. Expose both as sliders, because the right values differ between a matte fabric and a glass bottle, and a fixed default will look wrong on half a catalogue.

Composite: place the cutout on a background chosen per preset — a solid colour, a gradient, or an image the user supplies. Scale the subject so it occupies a configurable percentage of the frame and centre it against its own bounding box, not the original image's, so items photographed off-centre still line up with each other. Add an optional contact shadow generated from the alpha matte, offset and blurred.

Presets: a preset holds a background, a target aspect ratio, an output size, a subject-fill percentage and a margin. Ship presets for square marketplace listings, a tall social format, and a wide banner, and let the user define their own. One run applies every enabled preset to every input.

Review: a contact sheet of results with the source thumbnail alongside, so a bad cutout is obvious at a glance. Clicking one opens a full-size comparison and lets that single image be re-run with adjusted matte settings without redoing the batch.

Output: write to a folder per preset, keep the original filename, and write a sidecar JSON per image recording the model, matte settings and preset used, so a batch can be reproduced.

Out of scope: generating backgrounds with a diffusion model, any hosted API, mobile apps, and retouching tools beyond the matte controls.

faq.q: Can I bring anything over from Pixelcut?
faq.a: Only the images themselves. Pixelcut's templates and saved backgrounds are not exportable, so presets get rebuilt here, which takes a few minutes each. Nothing else is worth migrating.

faq.q: How good is the cutout compared to Pixelcut's?
faq.a: Close on solid subjects with clear edges, and worse on hair, fur, mesh and anything transparent. The erode-and-feather controls in the prompt exist specifically because the default output has a visible halo on light backgrounds, which is the difference you will notice first.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing after the model downloads. Everything runs locally on CPU at a few seconds per image, faster with a GPU. For a catalogue of a few hundred products this is a coffee break, once.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Doing it on the phone. Pixelcut's real workflow is photograph, tap, post, without the image ever reaching a computer. A folder-based desktop pipeline is a different habit, and for a lot of sellers it is the wrong one.
